content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on two player competitive games, in MuJoCo environments. The proposed method makes use of a dynamics model to find perturbations that maximize the difference between the two agent value functions in h steps time. This is an intuitive idea and would make a good paper if slightly better executed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

* The use of a learned dynamics model for adversarial robustness in continuous control seems well-motivated and sensible. 
* The story of the paper makes sense. 
* The motivation for h step prediction is sound. 

### Weaknesses

* The actual performance of the method is quite disappointing. For example, in Table 1 it is very hard to see how this method is any better than RADIAL. It might be, but it certainly isn't obvious from this. It could be a good idea to consider using the rliable library from Agarwal et al, and compute the IQM over all attacks for each environment. 
* The authors make a point about the ability to model multiple steps in the future, but it seems in Table 2 like the gains are by far the strongest for h=1, so just single step. Why is this?
* There is no analysis on the types of adversarial attacks proposed by this approach and how they differ vs. alternative approaces.
* What are the limitations of this method?
* Does this work outside of the MuJoCo environments shown?
* The paper appears rushed with multiple typos and poorly formatted components. This is fine but please improve during the discussion phase. For example, Figure 4 doesn't have any caption describing what is going on, and contains a significant amount of white space. Figure 5 is beyond the width of the paper. The fact the authors used less than 9 pages isn't a negative but is indicative that it was rushed. See minor issues below for more.
* There have been some related works in the offline RL setting, with a slightly different motivation. See the following:
    * Rigter et al. RAMBO-RL: Robust Adversarial Model-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning. NeurIPS 2022
    * Ball et al. Augmented World Models Facilitate Zero-Shot Dynamics Generalization From a Single Offline Environment. ICML 2021.

Minor issues:
* There are many cases where parentheses do not have a space after the text. E.g. this( instead of this (. For example p1 FGSM, p2 techniques.
* Sec 2.2 "our method directly utilize the gradients" -> "our method directly utilizes the gradients".
* Sec 4.2 "the role of dynamics model" -> "the role of a dynamics model".
* Sec 3 incorrect use of quotation marks in latex. This is a common mistake.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The idea seems novel to me, and fairly clearly presented.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is a weak reject because it is a nice idea, which is well motivated but 1) the experiments don't show strong gains 2) there is no analysis as to how/why/when this works 3) the paper appears rushed. With more time this could be a nice contribution to ICLR, I am curious to see what the authors have done since submission and how they plan to improve the paper during the discussion phase.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors study a somewhat _well-studied_ problem -- attacking reinforcement learning agents in two-player zero-sum game. The idea is to compute adversary vectors that perturb the observation so that the differences between the agent and the opponent's $V$ functions is maximized. The experiments are carried out on some Mujuco tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
__Related work__

The reviewer is mainly concerned about the poorly covered related work. The method under studied is ___not___ a unique one as claimed by the authors. The paper misses quite a few important references, both related to adversarial attacks in two-agent competitive RL. The reviewer lists a few papers here and notes that there are some other important references.

- Guo et al., Adversarial policy learning in two-player competitive games
- Wang et al., Backdoorl: Backdoor attack against competitive reinforcement learning

Evaluating the contributions of this work without having an adequate discussion on the related work is difficult.

__Attack model__

The attack model assumes that the opponent in the two-player game has the access to the agent's state, and some other information. This assumption is unrealistic in competitive settings.

The method seems to train the agent with earlier revealed information (or competition policy) of the opponent, because the opponent policy is the same in training- and testing- time and the method simply looks ahead for several steps. The reviewer is even not sure whether this method can be classified as an "robust learning" method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
__Quality__

1. There are many problems with the definition of problem settings.
- For a two-agent game, MDP is not a good model. Consider defining your settings as a two-player MDP.
- The authors state in previous sections that they study zero-sum games, but this is not defined in the setting.
- The definition of value function and policy learning objective is also problematic. There are two agents, so consider adding subscripts to make your definition rigorous.

2. How is the adversarial vector $\delta$ calculated?

The authors first said that $\delta$ is calculated by back-propagating the loss of value difference. However, it was then defined formally as $\delta=\epsilon\cdot \mathcal{sign}(\cdots)$. This is wired, given that $\epsilon$ is a factor controlling the attack budget, and $sign$ only changes the sign.


__Clarity__

1. $P: S \times A \rightarrow R$ denotes the probability of transition between two states. $P$ should be defined on $S \times A \times S$.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper lacks discussion of and comparison against many important related papers. The assumption of the attack method seems to be unrealistic. These two problems are the major drawbacks of the paper.

As for clarity, the reviewer is concerned that the paper, in its current status, is not rigorous enough to be published. The notations and definitions seem arbitrary.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

display_title: Official Review of Paper5580 by Reviewer G2Lv

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an adversarial defense method based on including a dynamics model to predict the effects of actions on the state, and thus be more resistant to perturbations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
* The paper aims at an important problem, of adversarial robustness
* The paper gives an interesting qualitative analysis of the You Shall Not Pass Experiment

Weaknesses:
* The main baseline, checking the adversarial robustness of a model-based RL algorithm, was not run.

Adding a dynamics model to the policy is an idea in model based RL outside of the context of adversarial robustness, and as such it would be better to frame this as a test of the robustness of dynamics-model-based rather than model free RL.  I would expect comparing this method to adversarial training of model based RL methods.

* The central concern of their adversarial perturbations not accounting for long-term effects would not occur at all in the Adversarial Policies model, which was done in the same environment, and thus should be compatible with this experimental setup.  Given that it should be confirmed that the issue being solved here is actually an issue when using an attack model that does long-term planning.

* The method appears to either not be very stable, or not very effective, due to the last ablation which shows that only 1 step ahead is useful, and performance diminishes after that.

* The statistical significance of the results in unclear, as it appears only one seed was run, and the methods are very close to the same performance.  The difference between methods could be attributable to hyper parameter tuning, but such tuning isn't discussed in the paper.

* The attack model is unclear
In some places the paper states that "adversarial perturbations are added to the adversaries behaviors" and implied by Figure 2 and Figure 3 it appears to imply that the perturbations are actually added to the adversaries actions, not just the victims observations of their actions.  However, in other places, such as Figure 4 it appears that the perturbations are only inserted into the victims observations of the adversaries actions.  These are two very different models!
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The setup of the paper is unclear in places, and thus seems difficult to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommending rejection of this paper, since the method should be compared against adversarial attacks which account for long term planing (like adversarial policies), and should be compared to RL approaches which already have dynamics models.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an adversarial training strategy against state perturbation attack which incorporates a trained dynamics model of the competivie RL environment. The perturbation is optimized to maximizes the differences between the value function of the attacker and the victim agent within a time window of $h$ steps. Numerical experiments on competitive MuJoCo environments are conducted to show the improved robustness of the training strategy againts various adversarial attacks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The incorporation of dynamics model to adversarial training for competitive RL is new.
- The adversarial training strategy is shown to be effective against various attacks.

Weaknesses:
- My first concern is about equation (5) where the perturbation is added to both the attacker and victim agents. Meanwhile, the authors mention that they only perturb the victim's state observation in Section 5.
- There are missing details on how the dynamics model are trained: how large is the training set, was normalization used? (otherwise the MSE loss will be dominated by certain subset of states)
- In equation (5), the authors use the dynamics model to sequentially predict the next state up to $h$ steps where error will be accumulated as we move further in the future. It may be good to discount the difference in the future in this case.
- The evaluation in 5.2 is only done under 1 noise level, it is better to have the results at multiple noise levels.

Minor comments:
- Typo at last paragraph on page 2: double "works"
- I think the algorithm in Madry et al. (2017) is FGSM not PGD.
- There are inconsistent usages of $V(\hat{s}_{t+1})$ and $\hat{V}(s_{t+1})$.
- Typo in equation (4): $\pi_{v_{old}}v(\cdot)$ should be $\pi_{v_{old}}(\cdot)$
- In equation (5) the step is denoted as $k$ while it is $h$ in earlier paragraphs.
- In Ablation Study paragraph, the rerefence to Table 5.2 should be Table 2.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written and easy to follow. The adversarial training scheme with the trained dynamics model for competitive RL is new to me. The code is provided for reproducibility which is a plus.
content.summary_of_the_review: My main concern is whether the authors perturb both attacker and victim as in equation (5) or only the victim as they claim in Section 5. I hope to see more clarification on this to better judge the results in Section 5. Also, the details on the training of dynamics model which is a key component in the proposed framework. There are also other minor issues which need to be revised as mentioned above.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
